interest: This file offers valuable insight into Japanese and Wang Ching-wei psychological warfare and intelligence operations in British Hong Kong during the Second Sino-Japanese War prior to the Pacific War. It illustrates the covert battle for public opinion and colonial tolerance, showing how collaborationist or Japanese agents attempted to pressure the British colonial administration and English-language media into expelling Nationalist (Chungking) figures. Furthermore, the enclosed list serves as a remarkable contemporary directory of Kuomintang high-level financial, intelligence, relief, and guerrilla support networks operating out of Hong Kong, featuring prominent members of the Soong family, Shanghai business and underworld figures such as Du Yuesheng (Doo Yu-wen), and senior diplomats and administrators.
overview: This file comprises Despatch No. 695 dated June 24, 1940, from Addison E. Southard, American Consul General in Hong Kong, to the Secretary of State, forwarding an anonymous letter circulated to Hong Kong's English-language press. Dated June 21, 1940, and signed 'A Native Born of Hongkong', the letter demands the immediate expulsion of eighteen prominent Chinese residents identified as 'Chungking agents' and 'anti-Japanese elements' conducting financial operations, secret service work, propaganda, and guerrilla coordination. Consul General Southard reports that local consensus attributes the letter to Japanese or Wang Ching-wei collaborationist sources, notes that local English newspapers had refrained from publishing it, and provides brief clarifying remarks regarding key individuals on the list, including Madame H. H. Kung (Soong Ai-ling) and T. V. Soong.

subfiles.about: American Consul General Addison E. Southard reports on an anonymous letter sent to Hong Kong English newspapers urging the expulsion of eighteen anti-Japanese Chinese figures.
subfiles.from: Addison E. Southard (American Consul General, Hong Kong)
subfiles.summary: Consul General Addison E. Southard transmits to the Secretary of State a confidential report regarding an anonymous letter addressed to English-language newspapers in Hong Kong. The letter demands the expulsion of eighteen well-known Chinese figures described as 'anti-Japanese elements' and Chungking agents. Southard notes that local observers consider the letter to originate from Japanese or Wang Ching-wei sources and that none of the English newspapers have published it. He also clarifies the identities and movements of several individuals on the list, noting that 'Soong Eh-lin' is Madame H. H. Kung (Soong Ai-ling) and that T. V. Soong was en route to or already in the United States.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 695 from Addison E. Southard on Japanese Propaganda and Expulsion List

subfiles.about: An anonymous letter addressed to Hong Kong's English press demanding the expulsion of eighteen prominent Chinese individuals active in anti-Japanese operations.
subfiles.from: 'A Native Born of Hongkong' (Post Office Box No. 14, Hong Kong)
subfiles.summary: An anonymous letter addressed to the editors of the English-language press in Hong Kong urges a campaign to expel eighteen named Chungking agents from the colony for the sake of Hong Kong's safety. The letter details the specific anti-Japanese functions of each individual, covering finance, secret service, intelligence, propaganda, Red Cross fundraising, and guerrilla warfare coordination. Among those listed are prominent political and economic figures including T. V. Soong, Doo Yu-wen (Du Yuesheng), C. T. Wang, O. K. Yui, T. A. Soong, and Soong Eh-lin (Soong Ai-ling).
subfiles.title: Enclosure: Anonymous Letter to the English Press Listing Chinese Notables to be Expelled
subfiles.to: Editors of all the English Press in Hong Kong
